subject: film
title: French New Wave (c. 1958–64): the camera leaves the studio
dek: Truffaut, Godard, Varda as a peer — auteurs, jump cuts, and Paris as a location, not a set.

thumb.alt: Agnès Varda standing on a wooden structure over water, early 1960s.

hero.alt: Rue Soufflot in Paris looking toward the Panthéon, late 1950s, with pedestrians and parked cars.
hero.caption: Rue Soufflot, toward the Panthéon, around the end of the 1950s. New Wave films treated streets like this as the set: available light, real traffic, a city that did not have to be rebuilt on a soundstage.

honesty: “Nouvelle Vague” was a press label before it was a school. The people in this capsule argued in Cahiers du Cinéma, then made films that did not look like the “tradition of quality” they had been attacking. This capsule looks out from Paris. Japanese New Wave and British Free Cinema are happening in the same years — not assigned Asian or British “peers.”

timeline.label: Cahiers
timeline.detail: Truffaut’s “Une certaine tendance du cinéma français”; the politique des auteurs is a fight about who authors a film.

timeline.label: Varda
timeline.detail: La Pointe Courte — often called a New Wave film before the name. She is a peer, not a guest.

timeline.label: Cannes
timeline.detail: Les Quatre Cents Coups. Truffaut the critic becomes Truffaut the director in public.

timeline.label: Breathless
timeline.detail: À bout de souffle. Jump cuts, handheld, a plot that refuses to behave.

timeline.label: Cléo
timeline.detail: Cléo de 5 à 7. Two hours in a city, a woman walking, time as a structure.

timeline.label: Elsewhere
timeline.detail: Japanese New Wave; Free Cinema and the British New Wave. Later cousin, not contemporaneous: Taiwan New Cinema in the 1980s.

glossary.explain: Press name, late 1950s, for a cluster of mostly young French directors who had often been critics first. It is a useful label and a bad census: people were included, excluded, and later added.
French film magazine, founded 1951. Truffaut, Godard, Chabrol, Rivette, Rohmer wrote there. The magazine was a school and a weapon.

Cahiers argument: a director can be the author of a film the way a novelist is the author of a book — including in Hollywood, if the films have a signature. In English this hardened into “auteur theory.” It was a polemic, not a law of nature.
Truffaut’s hostile name for the polished, literary, studio-bound French cinema of the 1940s–50s that Cahiers wanted to replace. “Quality” here is an insult.
An edit that skips a bit of time inside a continuous shot, so the image jerks. Breathless made the device famous as style, not as a mistake to be hidden.
Lightweight French 35mm camera (Éclair). New Wave crews used cameras like this because they could leave the studio. Portability is an aesthetic with a serial number.
Later grouping of filmmakers including Varda, Resnais, Marker — often more essayistic or Left Bank geographically and temperamentally than the Cahiers men. Useful, and too neat.
British mid-1950s documentary movement (Anderson, Reisz, Richardson and others): short films, everyday subjects, a manifesto. It is contemporaneous, not a French export.
Japanese 1960s directors (Oshima, Imamura, Teshigahara and others) breaking with studio form. The name borrows the French phrase. The films do not.
U.S. late-1960s/1970s studio crash and youth-market turn. Bonnie and Clyde (1967) is the usual bridge sentence from the New Wave. A later effect, not a twin.
1980s Taiwanese film movement (Hou Hsiao-hsien, Edward Yang, and others). A later cousin in the family of “new cinemas,” not a 1960 contemporary.
The festival that, in 1959, made Les Quatre Cents Coups an international event. A prize is not a movement, but it is how a movement gets a date.

fun_fact.title: The jump cuts were also a budget
fun_fact.text: Godard and editor Cécile Decugis shortened Breathless by cutting inside shots, not only between them. The jump cut is now taught as a philosophy of time. It was also a way to lose running time without reshooting Paris. Both things can be true: a device can be an idea and a solution to a reel that was too long.

sections.title: Critics with a grudge, and a camera that could walk

blocks.text: In the 1950s a set of Paris critics used Cahiers du Cinéma to pick a fight with their own national cinema. Truffaut’s 1954 essay “Une certaine tendance du cinéma français” attacked what he called the tradition of quality: well-upholstered literary adaptations, studio craft, a cinema that looked finished and felt, to him, dead. The politique des auteurs was the other half of the fight. A director, even in Hollywood, could be an author. Hitchcock counted. So did Hawks. The insult to the French studio system was the point.

blocks.alt: An Éclair Cameflex 35mm movie camera on a tripod, labeled Eclair Paris and Chevereau.
blocks.caption: An Éclair Cameflex, the kind of relatively light 35mm camera Paris rental houses such as Chevereau supplied. New Wave form is often taught as an idea. It is also a kit that could be carried into a street.

blocks.text: They were not the first people to want a camera outside. Italian neorealism had already taken the war’s rubble as a set. What was new in Paris was the combination: critics who became directors, a magazine that had already trained an audience, and equipment that made a low budget look like a choice.

sections.title: 1959 is a date. It is not the whole map.

blocks.text: Les Quatre Cents Coups premiered at Cannes in 1959. Truffaut, who had been banned from the festival as a critic, arrived as a director. The film follows Antoine Doinel through a Paris that is not a postcard — school, streets, a runaway, a freeze-frame on a beach. It is the date the press needed. It is not the first film in the cluster.

blocks.alt: Paris street toward the Panthéon, late 1950s.
blocks.caption: The Latin Quarter as a working street, not a back lot. New Wave location shooting made Paris look like a place people already lived — which is why the city in these films still feels like itself, and why a production still needed permits, light, and luck.

blocks.text: À bout de souffle (1960) is the film people mean when they say “jump cut.” Godard and his editor cut inside shots; time skips; the hero talks to the camera as if the fourth wall were optional. The plot is a thin crime story. The event is the grammar.

Agnès Varda is not a cameo in a men’s movement. La Pointe Courte (1955) is often called a New Wave film before the name existed. Cléo de 5 à 7 (1962) walks a singer through two real-time hours of Paris while she waits for a medical result. If “auteur” only fits the Cahiers men, the word is too small — the same problem a later feminism lesson will have with “first wave.”

blocks.alt: Agnès Varda, short dark hair, standing with another woman on a wooden deck over water.
blocks.caption: Agnès Varda (left), early 1960s. The filename on this archive print says Venice, 1962 — the year of Cléo. Treat the place-name as the archive’s label. The person is not in doubt: a director who was already working when the magazine men picked up cameras.

blocks.alt: Children looking through a professional motion-picture camera on a tripod, with an adult nearby.
blocks.caption: A later photograph of a portable camera on a tripod, children looking through the finder. This is not a 1959 production still. It is here because the New Wave’s bet — that a lighter camera changes who gets to shoot, and where — did not stay in Paris. The kit traveled. The date of this picture is later than the era. The idea is the era’s.

blocks.text: The same years, elsewhere: in Japan, Oshima, Imamura, Teshigahara and others were breaking studio form; the Japanese phrase nūberu bāgu borrows the French name and then goes its own way. In Britain, Free Cinema’s shorts and manifesto (Anderson, Reisz, Richardson) had already argued for everyday subjects and a camera that did not owe the studio a polished lie. These are contemporaneous arguments, not a seating chart with France at the head.

people.name: François Truffaut
people.text: Critic, then director. Les Quatre Cents Coups made the movement a Cannes story. He kept coming back to Antoine Doinel. The man who attacked the tradition of quality became, in time, a tradition of his own — which is a later capsule.

people.name: Jean-Luc Godard
people.text: À bout de souffle, then a career of breaking the toy he had just been given. Jump cuts are the textbook; the longer fact is a director who treated cinema as an argument that could be continued in public.

people.name: Agnès Varda
people.caption: A peer, not a supporting role.
people.text: Photographer first, then filmmaker. La Pointe Courte, Cléo, and decades of work after the New Wave name had gone cold. If a syllabus puts her in a sidebar, the syllabus is the artifact.

sections.title: Who gets to be the author

blocks.text: The politique des auteurs was a way of watching Hollywood with respect and watching French “quality” with contempt. It gave critics a hero: the director as signature. It also made it easy to miss the editor, the cinematographer, the producer, the actor who is carrying the film. Breathless without Raoul Coutard’s camera, or without Jean Seberg’s face, is a different object. Varda’s career is a useful correction: the author can be a woman who was never on the Cahiers masthead as a boy critic.
Keep the Cameflex in mind. Authorship, in this era, is also a question of who can afford to leave the studio, and who is allowed to.

sections.title: New Hollywood, and a cousin who arrives late

blocks.text: American studios in the late 1960s needed a younger audience and had lost the old Production Code’s certainty. Bonnie and Clyde (1967) is the sentence film histories use to connect Paris to New Hollywood. The connection is real and incomplete. A lot of other things — television, the draft, the collapse of the studio system’s weekly habit — were in that room.

Taiwan New Cinema, in the 1980s, is sometimes filed as another “new wave.” It is a later cousin: a different state, a different language politics, a different argument with its own studios. It does not belong on the 1958–64 timeline except as a reminder that the French name traveled, and that travel is not the same as origin.
If the director is the author, whose names have to wait in the credits?
